name: Hinman Booking Website
description: The public website for a local music booking business, built as the first piece of a larger booking platform (archived demo).

pageContent.text: Hinman Booking was the website for a small business that booked local musicians with local venues. I built it in mid-2024 with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Sass, had a working site deployed in about a week, and later turned it into a Progressive Web App. It was only ever shared with a handful of the musicians and venues the owner already worked with.

The public site was meant to be the first piece of a much larger booking platform, possibly split into a public site and a separate dashboard. The owner would create venues and bookings, and users would create one or more Artist profiles, since one person might play solo and in several bands. I kept the term "Artist" broad on purpose so it could fit however people used the service. From their profiles, artists would manage current and past bookings, request new ones, and browse an events board where the owner posted open bookings, showing each artist only the ones that matched their budget, style of music, and instrumentation. I started on that dashboard in early 2025, but the details were never fully worked out before the business closed.

Until that system existed, booking worked the old-fashioned way: the booking page lists the forms an artist needs to download, fill out, and email back. It was always meant as a stopgap. Behind the scenes, the contact form sent email through Nodemailer with sanitize-html cleaning the input, and Prisma was set up for the PostgreSQL database the accounts would eventually need.

images.alt: Hinman Booking page listing the three forms artists need to submit, with a W-9 download card over a dimly lit drum kit

pageContent.text: The part I'm least proud of is authentication. Over about two months I started with NextAuth, switched to a custom JWT and cookie setup, went back to NextAuth, tried Lucia, then removed it all and started NextAuth over again. I kept reading pros and cons instead of making a decision. The business eventually closed for reasons that had nothing to do with the site, but auth still wasn't settled when it did. The lesson stuck: today I'd try an option in a short spike, pick one, and commit to it, because switching back and forth burns time without moving the product forward.

When the business closed, the owner gave me permission to keep the site as a portfolio piece. I turned off outgoing email, replaced his contact details and private documents with placeholders, and left the rest as it was when work stopped. The photos are stock images from Pexels and Pixabay or early AI-generated images, meant to be replaced with real bands and venues. The landing page is unfinished too: its lower sections were designed to hold much more than the text that's there now. I've kept it this way as an honest look at a project mid-build.

name: Franklin Pearl & The Moon Website
description: A prototype website for my band, built as a Progressive Web App in 2022 and revived in 2026.

pageContent.text: Franklin Pearl & The Moon is a local band I play keys in, and this site was one of my earliest front-end projects. I built it over a few weeks in May and June 2022 as a prototype of what a band website could look like. The band hasn't decided it needs a website yet, so for now it stays a prototype.

It's built with Next.js 12 and React, styled with CSS Modules and React Bootstrap, and set up as a Progressive Web App with next-pwa so fans could install it on their phones. The homepage introduces the band members, features two songs, and shows a "Next Up" card for the upcoming gig, with a Shows page listing the rest. The play buttons next to the two songs were meant to play a pair of hardcoded tracks using the browser's built-in audio, no music service required.

images.alt: Franklin Pearl & The Moon homepage with band member photos, song previews, and a Next Up show card for Arrow Bar

pageContent.text: The feature I was most excited about never got built. The plan was a protected page where we could enter a show's title, start and end time, location, description, and an optional cover charge, then generate a QR code from it. Anyone interested in coming could scan the code and have the event added to their phone's calendar. The Next Up card still has the one static QR code from that time, made for a single show at Arrow Bar.

Our drummer is also into graphic design, so we planned to design products and sell them through a Redbubble store, with the newest designs shown on the homepage. The store was created but never stocked, which is why the merch section still uses placeholder images. Rather than send visitors to an empty store, I've since pointed the Merch link back to the homepage, along with the "Listen to More" link, since we never set up a SoundCloud account either.

In August 2026 I brought the project back to life. Node 16 had reached end of life, so I moved it to Node 24, fixed a next-pwa config error that broke the build, worked around a Next.js image loader bug, and shrank a 17 MB image down to 1.4 MB to clear the PWA's precache warnings. I also removed dead routes and leftover Heroku scripts, and replaced a generic third-party privacy policy with an honest one that reflects what the site actually collects: nothing.

name: Juicy Tales Website
description: The official website for Juicy Tales' poems, prose, and stories

pageContent.text: Juicy Tales is a client website prototype for an author who likes to write prose, stories, and occasionally lyrics for music. The prototype was never finished before the project got canceled, but I was given permission to use it as a portfolio piece.

This project was a new type of challenge for me: an audiovisual storytelling system, where a story plays out letter-by-letter across a music track for an emotional undercurrent. The client wanted it to reflect how he wrote: one segment at a time on its own card. He had a pile of cards that were numbered, and he would read them sequentially. The dramatic pauses between cards gave a heaviness I thought we could emulate for a more dramatic effect.

images.alt: The Carnival Mind poem page on Juicy Tales, with the opening lines above a dark, gothic illustration

pageContent.text: The site was created with React and TypeScript using the Next.js metaframework, with Tailwind for styling. There were plans to incorporate the Prisma ORM atop a PostgreSQL database for storing the writings and site settings.
It makes heavy use of the `typewriter-effect` package for the actual display of the story content, with `react-use-audio-player` and `framer-motion` for controlling the more audiovisual aspects.

name: KC Land & Stump Website
description: The website for a family land clearing business, with a custom admin panel for managing its own photos and pages.

pageContent.text: KC Land & Stump is the website for my dad Kelly's land clearing business in Atlanta, TX, built to advertise his services and give the company an online presence. The site was originally built in 2024 with Next.js, and was later rebuilt from the ground up in 2026 with TanStack Start.

I switched frameworks for two reasons: overhead, and a chance to learn. Next.js is great for many things, but it was overkill for what was then a handful of static pages, and choosing a stack that fit the project from the start was my biggest lesson here. I was already learning TanStack Start, so migrating the site while revamping it felt like a natural step.

images.alt: KC Land & Stump services page with photo cards for stump grinding, land clearing, dirt work, gravel spreading, and hauling

pageContent.text: While the original site was live, Kelly often asked me to swap in photos from new jobs. He needed more than a photo gallery; he needed control over his own content. So I built a protected admin interface where he can upload photos, choose where they appear, and edit his pages with drafts before publishing. Behind it, Prisma and PostgreSQL store the data, and every upload is resized and stripped of metadata like GPS location before it's stored.

images.alt: KC Land & Stump admin editor for the Hauling & Delivery page, with editable text, photo swapping, and draft and publish controls

pageContent.text: Resizing images, working with object storage, stripping metadata, and building a small custom CMS were all new to me in this redesign. The biggest takeaway was how much a simple content tool can change things for a client: Kelly can now keep his site current on his own, and it reflects his work as it happens.

name: Stegaveil CLI
description: A command-line tool that hides messages inside images, with optional password-based encryption and a browser demo that runs the real CLI.

pageContent.text: Stegaveil started in May 2025 as "Stegaboo." I'd been working through Typer CLI tutorials while experimenting with steganography on the side, so combining the two felt like a natural first command-line project. It was also my first project built with AI from the very start, which made it as much about learning to direct AI-written code as about the code itself.

Steganography hides the fact that a message exists at all, while cryptography makes a message unreadable without hiding it. Stegaveil does both. It writes each bit of a message into the lowest bit of a pixel's red, green, and blue values, a change too small for the eye to notice, and it can optionally encrypt the message first so it stays unreadable even if someone finds it.

images.alt: Stegaveil running in the browser, encoding a quote into an image and then decoding it back out

pageContent.text: When I came back to it in 2026, the playful Stegaboo branding no longer fit, and neither did some of its internals: messages were stored as plain text, ended with a marker string a message could accidentally contain, and had no encryption at all. I rebuilt it from scratch as Stegaveil. Each message now starts with a small header recording its length, so any text decodes correctly, and optional encryption uses AES-256-GCM with a key derived from your password by Argon2id. A wrong password or a tampered image fails loudly instead of returning garbage.

To make it easy to try, I added a [live demo](https://jnxvln.github.io/stegaveil/) that runs the actual Python package in the browser through WebAssembly, so nothing you upload leaves your device. Getting it working meant handling details like Argon2's use of multiple threads, which the browser's Python runtime doesn't support.

Stegaveil isn't meant for serious secrecy: simple least-significant-bit hiding can be detected with statistical analysis. What it gave me was a lesson in the difference between code that works and code I understand, and going back through a project I hadn't written by hand is what turned it into one I can explain.

name: CHLM Website
description: The public website for a landscaping materials supplier, with a filterable product catalog, a coverage calculator, and store notices managed from the internal dashboard.

pageContent.text: C&H Landscape Materials (CHLM) is a family business, and its website is one of my longest-running projects. I started it soon after I began working there in 2019, with the goal of showing off the materials we sell, but it grew in scope quickly.

images.alt: CHLM materials page filtered to Gravel / Rock, showing gravel cards with sizes, bin numbers, descriptions, and tags

pageContent.text: Based on customer interactions in the office, I realized site visitors wanted a way to narrow down what they were looking for, more detailed information about the products, and a way to estimate how much material they'd need for bulk products. So I built a more organized menu with tags and filtering, a searchable help page with a FAQ section, and an interactive project calculator.

images.alt: Project calculator estimating material for a circle border, with the result in cubic yards and loader buckets

pageContent.text: At one point the website even showed our live material inventory. Management later asked for it to be taken down, but since I'd built it as a toggle in the internal dashboard, turning it off took one click. The dashboard also controls the notices customers see, like the seasonal Saturday closure. That taught me to build features so they can change without a rewrite.

images.alt: CHLM homepage showing a Saturday closure notice set from the internal dashboard

pageContent.text: Employee workflow needs inside our small office grew as well. I noticed repeating patterns such as having to hand-write formulas on the pages we stapled bills to, manually recording and keeping track of truckload hauls, and other repetitive tasks. I realized some automation could help, so I began creating a separate, internal company dashboard (see [CHLM Dashboard](/projects/chlm2025-dashboard-qwik)) to help us manage day-to-day office work, and eventually [FleetTrack](/projects/fleettrack), which tracks driver mileage and fuel usage and generates useful reports.
These three projects taught me more than how to code: they taught me to build around real business needs, spot where automation helps, and plan for what's coming next.

name: Jnxvln Portfolio 2026
description: A deliberately simple portfolio that puts my projects front and center, with deeper write-ups for anyone who wants the details.

pageContent.text: In some ways, creating this portfolio has been more challenging than building applications for clients. The features and designs of client work arise from their needs and preferences, whereas creating this portfolio has involved making decisions entirely on my own, which, for some reason, has been harder to do.

Curating and presenting my work to the public has been an interesting experience, and one that involves a great deal of vulnerability. Though I've been dabbling with programming since the age of 13, I only started building it into a valuable skill set well into my 20s. I learned I can use these skills to help others gain more presence online, automate parts of their workflow, and provide tools that help them better understand their business.

As for this portfolio itself, I've kept it simple on purpose. The goal is to present, not distract: to put the important information up front while tucking the finer details away for those who want to dig deeper. Thinking from the point of view of whoever will be using an application has taught me how to make a more meaningful impact.

images.alt: Portfolio projects page with a tag filter, sort menu, and project cards showing tech stack tags and links

pageContent.text: It's my hope that this portfolio isn't just an aid to my résumé, but also serves as an ongoing testament to my developer experience as I continue to learn and grow.

name: PunchKit (ESP32)
description: A custom RFID employee timeclock built from scratch on the ESP32, with OLED screen and buzzer feedback.

pageContent.text: PunchKit is an experiment in creating my first useful electronics device, beyond simply learning how to make LEDs blink or buzzers go off.

I first delved into electronics in 2025, having picked up an Arduino kit and worked through examples in the book. I became intrigued and wanted to learn more. Eventually, I began to feel more confident that I could create something small, I just wasn't sure what. At that time in the office where I worked, I noticed some recurring patterns in employees' hand-written timesheets: missing entries, miscalculated hours, etc. and I thought this would be the perfect situation to help with.

Some years prior, I had suggested to my employer that we look into a timekeeping system, but the interest never really escalated. So I asked if I could try to come up with my own solution which would be cheaper and (hopefully) just as efficient, and help me learn at the same time. They said yes, and that is how this project began.

The prototype is an ESP32 on a breadboard with an RC522 RFID reader, a small SSD1306 OLED screen, a DS3231 real-time clock, and a buzzer. Scanning a registered fob or card clocks that employee in or out based on their current status, and the screen shows their name, IN or OUT, and the time. Each result gets its own beep pattern, so it's clear without looking whether a punch worked, came from the admin card, or came from an unknown card. A short cooldown keeps a single tap from punching twice. The clock stores UTC and converts to local time with one offset constant, so a daylight saving change is a one-line edit. I also reworked the buzzer, screen, and cooldown to use non-blocking timing, so the device stays responsive instead of freezing while a beep plays.

images.alt: ESP32 board on a red breakout PCB next to a small display showing live temperature, humidity, and pressure readings

pageContent.text: It's still a work in progress, and the rest is planned. Punches will be saved to a database, or possibly synced to Google Sheets, instead of only being shown on screen. Fobs and cards will be registered and unregistered from the device, and the admin card will trigger a timesheet report on a small dashboard. Last comes an enclosure that keeps moisture out while still letting heat escape. It's been a fun way to learn electronics, and it's headed toward something the office can actually use.

name: CHLM Dashboard
description: An internal operations dashboard built for a landscaping and materials supply company, handling everything from driver and vendor management to freight billing and daily haul tracking.

pageContent.text: The CHLM Dashboard is internal software I built for C&H Landscape Materials (CHLM) to handle the office's day-to-day work.

The need for automation, precise calculations, and generating reports grew the longer I worked at C&H. I started noticing repetitive patterns within our office work. Up until then, my time as a developer was mostly front-end, but I started realizing I could use those skills to make life easier in the office. I don't think I realized at that time just how useful that would become.

At first, the focus was getting a navigable site up and running. The office was busy every day, so getting an MVP in front of staff quickly was vital. However, it was also the foundation, so I knew it needed to be solid. Earlier iterations of the dashboard helped shape what routes I already knew I needed, such as Drivers, Workdays, Hauls, and Vendors. I knew the biggest chunk of time and work would be implementing the Haul system, where we enter our drivers' daily trip sheet information. However, for that to work, the database schema needed a chain of dependencies: a Haul requires a Workday and a Driver, for example. A Haul also needs a Vendor Product, which requires a Vendor, and so on. Getting those relationships right was challenging and tedious, but it was essential for creating a robust system that could grow with time.

images.alt: CHLM Dashboard hauls view filtered by driver and date, with workdays expanded to show each haul's route, material, and tonnage

pageContent.text: Once the MVP was up and running and usable within the office, I was able to breathe a bit. I began adding features like pagination and sorting, tightening form validation rules, implementing a soft-deletion system (so my co-workers couldn't accidentally delete important records permanently), adding a Waiting List (for customers waiting on materials), and more. Over time, the application started growing tremendously, causing me to split off a major trucking-related portion into its own app ([FleetTrack](/projects/fleettrack)), and I knew some housekeeping was in order.

The codebase had grown beyond what I could easily keep track of on my own, and I needed some help. By this point I had already been tinkering with AI in smaller projects, so I instructed it to perform a full-blown audit across my codebase, giving me a bird's-eye view and helping me determine where my best effort was needed. It pointed out things like a health check endpoint that exposed more than it needed to and a login with no throttling against repeated attempts. For nearly two months I worked on cleanup and security hardening: field-level encryption for personal information, password hardening, login throttling, and tooling to rotate encryption keys if that ever became necessary. That turned out to be timely: in 2026, a major database service provider was breached. My project wasn't affected, but it drove home how essential security is.

images.alt: CHLM Dashboard demo login page, with a public demo banner and the demo credentials shown

pageContent.text: With the hardening done, I created a public demo of the Dashboard in a sandboxed environment, filled with seed data that resets automatically, for code reviewers and interviewers to explore. If you're interested, check out the [CHLM Dashboard Demo](https://chlm2025dashboardqwik-portfolio-demo.up.railway.app/).

Beyond that, I built controls into the dashboard that update the separate CHLM public website (see the [CHLM Website](/projects/chlm2025-website) project), automating things like seasonal store hours and weather-related closure notices. This was the project where I really learned to build software, and I'm still improving it today as new needs come up in the office.

images.alt: Dashboard website notices page listing notices that appear on the public CHLM homepage, with type, display dates, and status

name: CHLM FleetTrack
description: An internal fleet tool for C&H Landscape Materials that tracks daily truck mileage and fuel receipts, flags problem entries, and generates printable fuel reports.

pageContent.text: CHLM FleetTrack is an internal, employee-only application for C&H Landscape Materials. It began as part of the [CHLM Dashboard](/projects/chlm2025-dashboard-qwik), but as the trucking side of the business grew, it needed a home of its own. Because it holds internal company data, the source code and live application aren't publicly available.

Each day, the office records the miles driven and fuel receipts for every truck in the fleet, to help management prepare for [IFTA](https://www.iftach.org/) reporting. FleetTrack keeps track of the trucks and fuel stations we use and offers autocomplete when entering receipts.

I knew management would want a way to total each truck's data by state, since IFTA reporting is broken down that way, so I built a reports page with preset date ranges (daily through yearly) plus custom ranges. To maximize room on the printable report, I included a state selector as well as toggleable columns. As a small quality-of-life touch, the "End-Dump" preset button automatically deselects all states, reselecting only the states our end-dump drivers most commonly drive in. The states included in that preset are separately configurable.

images.alt: FleetTrack reports page with period, truck, state, and column filters above a weekly fleet report broken down by state

pageContent.text: Paper receipts aren't always perfect, nor are handwritten report annotations, so I added a field-flagging system: any field can be marked as missing, illegible, or incorrect, and flagged items are grouped in their own report so they can be followed up on and corrected.

images.alt: FleetTrack entry form with a missing mileage field flagged in red

pageContent.text: Data collection, filtering, and presentation are the heart of FleetTrack and will continue to improve as the company grows, offering more opportunities for me to learn and adapt as needs change.
